name: Splitting the Bills
description: Settle up a flat share: rent by room size, flatmates moving in and out mid-month, a Netflix share some opted out of, council tax with student and single-person rules, a boiler repair one person caused, standing orders and money already sent, and a corrected bill. Every balance and every transfer is checked to the penny against an exact calculator.
hook: Who owes whom, to the penny, when everyone moved in on different days?
author: Gauntlet Real-World Pack

cases.prompt:
Hi! Our flat needs to settle up for Wed 1 Apr to Tue 30 Jun 2026 (both days included) and I want it exactly right. Here’s everything.

FLATMATES
Name | Room size | Lived here | Student? | In the Netflix share?
Rosa | 12 m² | Wed 1 Apr – Tue 30 Jun | no | -
Joanna | 12 m² | Wed 1 Apr – Tue 30 Jun | no | -
Wen | 12 m² | Wed 1 Apr – Tue 30 Jun | no | -
A day counts for someone if they lived here that day (first and last days included).

HOW WE SPLIT THINGS (agreed rules)
- Rent is £1,650.00 a calendar month for the whole flat. Each day’s rent (that month’s rent ÷ the number of days in the month) is shared by the people living here that day, in proportion to their room sizes.
- Broadband is £36.00 a calendar month. Each day’s broadband (month ÷ days in the month) is shared equally by the people living here that day.
- Each energy bill covers the dates shown. Each day of a bill (bill ÷ days it covers) is shared equally by the people living here that day.

BILLS AND WHO PAID THEM
- Rosa paid the landlord the rent for every month.
- Everyone else pays Rosa a standing order on the 1st of every month on which they live here: Joanna £550.00, Wen £550.00.
- Joanna paid the broadband every month.
- Electricity and gas, 1 Apr – 30 Jun: £418.35, paid by Wen.

Work out each person’s balance: everything they paid (to the landlord, suppliers or engineer, plus money they sent to flatmates) minus their fair share of everything, minus money flatmates sent them. A positive balance means they are owed money. Keep exact amounts throughout and round each balance to the nearest penny only at the end.
Then settle up with as few bank transfers as possible, using our method (it makes the answer unique): the person who owes the most pays the person who is owed the most, as much as possible (the smaller of the two amounts); repeat until everyone is square. If two people owe (or are owed) exactly the same, take them in alphabetical order.

Answer in this JSON format (amounts in pounds, two decimals; list the transfers in the order the method makes them):
```json
{"balances": {"<name>": 0.00}, "transfers": [{"from": "<name>", "to": "<name>", "amount": 0.00}]}
```
Give exactly one answer as a single JSON block. Do not offer alternatives: a reply that contains two different answers, or an answer that says "or", is marked wrong. You may explain your working before the JSON.
cases.notes: [easy] Exact shares (fractions) rounded only at the end: Rosa -£175.45, Joanna -£67.45, Wen £242.90 (sum £0.00). Settle-up by the stated method, 2 transfers = the proven minimum: Rosa→Wen £175.45; Joanna→Wen £67.45. Generator attempt 3.
